notes.text:
# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 [tentative]
At fixed reagent and liquid volumes, anonymous solvent–extractant pairing changes the equilibrium target allocation between organic and aqueous phases. Because the catalog supplies no properties, no label ordering is assumed. Initial test: screen structured pairings with identical mixing and phase amounts; a reproducible material effect should exceed stated measurement noise and survive a cross-pair check.

## H2 [tentative]
For a fixed promising material pair, increasing the organic share should increase the fraction of the batch target inventory in the organic phase, while the inferred concentration-based distribution tendency may remain approximately stable. Testable consequence: product_in_organic rises with organic volume fraction, but an inferred distribution coefficient from both-phase fractions is less variable.

## H3 [tentative]
Mixing affects approach to equilibrium rather than the equilibrium partition itself: inadequate mixing should change observed allocation, whereas sufficiently strong/long mixing should plateau. This will be tested using deliberately contrasting mixing conditions, with settling held explicit.

## Measurement/decision plan
Use one pre-separation HPLC per batch to observe both-phase fractions, then physically retain a phase, terminate, and obtain the required final assay. Organic will usually be retained, with selected aqueous retention used to test phase accounting. Numerical differences will not be called effects without considering declared instrument noise, confounding, and repeatability. Conditions may be adapted only after measured evidence; anonymous IDs remain categorical.

# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 [supported for screened conditions; interaction unresolved]
With 0.03 L solvent, 0.03 L aqueous addition, 0.03 L extractant, and 120 s/600 rpm mixing, material labels substantially change allocation. Holding X0 fixed, pre-separation organic fractions were about 0.195 (S0), 0.378 (S1), 0.267 (S2), and 0.431 (S3) (events runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, -0037; HPLC SD 0.015). Thus the S3–S0 numerical contrast is much larger than single-measurement noise. Holding S3 fixed, X0 gave about 0.431 versus 0.362, 0.368, and 0.348 for X1–X3 (events -0037, -0047, -0057, -0067). The X1/X2/X3 ordering is unresolved at this precision. No anonymous label ordering or real identity is inferred.

A remaining alternative is solvent–extractant interaction rather than additive categorical effects. Planned pre-experiment cross-check: S1/X2 completes a 2×2 subset with observed S1/X0, S3/X0, S3/X2. A departure from the additive contrast beyond measurement scatter would support interaction.

## H2 [tentative; follow-up specified]
At S3/X0, change added organic material while keeping chemistry and mixing fixed. Low-organic test: 0.015 L solvent + 0.015 L extractant + 0.03 L aqueous addition. High-organic test: 0.04 L solvent + 0.04 L extractant + 0.01 L aqueous addition. Prediction made before these experiments: pre-separation product_in_organic and phase_ratio increase from low to high. I will also compute an apparent distribution ratio D=(f_org/V_org)/(f_aq/V_aq) using the measured phase_ratio; approximate constancy would support simple equilibrium partitioning, while systematic change would expose composition dependence or model inadequacy.

## H3 [tentative; follow-up specified]
At baseline S3/X0 and volumes, compare 1 s/100 rpm with 600 s/1200 rpm against the 120 s/600 rpm observation (event -0037). Prediction made before tests: the weak condition may under-equilibrate; the baseline and high condition should be closer if a plateau exists. A monotone change through all three would instead leave equilibrium unresolved.

## Measurement interpretation
HPLC is taken before phase removal and reports fractions of fixed initial target inventory, not concentrations. Final assays after phase retention are used as phase-accounting checks and are not treated as interchangeable with the pre-separation readings. Selected aqueous retention (batch 2) gave final aqueous target about 0.657 after pre-separation aqueous about 0.653 (events -0017, -0020), consistent within assay noise; nonzero signals in removed phases are treated as sampling/noise rather than missing values or exact zeros.

notes.text:
# Partition study — final source-stage notebook

## H1 [supported for material effects in the screened scope; interaction unresolved]
At common phase additions and 120 s/600 rpm mixing, changing solvent at X0 shifted pre-separation organic target fraction from about 0.195 (S0) through 0.267 (S2), 0.378 (S1), to 0.431 (S3) (events runner-operation-0007, -0027, -0017, -0037; declared HPLC SD 0.015). Changing extractant at S3 gave 0.431 (X0), 0.362 (X1), 0.368 (X2), and 0.348 (X3) (events -0037, -0047, -0057, -0067). Thus broad material effects are supported, but close rankings are not.

The 2×2 cross-check gave S1/X2 = 0.366 (event -0117), versus S1/X0 = 0.378, S3/X0 = 0.431, and S3/X2 = 0.368. The difference-of-differences is about -0.051; with four independent HPLC readings each having stated SD 0.015, this is suggestive but not decisive and there is no replication. Pair interaction remains unresolved rather than rejected. Anonymous IDs are independent categories and no numeric ordering or real identity is assigned.

## H2 [supported qualitatively; simple constant-D model only approximate]
For S3/X0 at 120 s/600 rpm, low, baseline, and high organic additions produced measured phase ratios 0.228, 0.327, 0.438 and organic inventory fractions 0.332, 0.431, 0.526 (events -0077, -0037, -0087). This supports the preregistered directional phase-amount prediction. Apparent D=(f_org/V_org)/(f_aq/V_aq), using measured phase ratio and both inventory fractions, was about 1.74, 1.58, and 1.48. The modest systematic drift could reflect composition-dependent partitioning because solvent and extractant amounts changed together with phase amount; a constant-D dilution law is therefore an approximation, not established.

## H3 [initial plateau claim rejected; mass transfer remains important]
At baseline S3/X0 volumes, organic fraction was 0.387 after 1 s/100 rpm, 0.431 after 120 s/600 rpm, and 0.555 after 600 s/1200 rpm (events -0097, -0037, -0107). The high-minus-baseline difference (~0.124) is far above the declared single-reading HPLC SD, so the proposed baseline/high plateau was not observed. Duration and speed were changed jointly, preventing attribution to either factor. These data support mixing-dependent approach/transport within the tested window but do not identify equilibrium or its kinetics.

## Phase retention and accounting
HPLC readings cited above were acquired before separation and represent both phases. `separate_phase` was treated as destructive removal of the nonrequested phase. Selected checks are consistent with retention within sampling/noise: batch 10 retained aqueous (pre 0.624 at -0097; final 0.643 at -0100), while batch 11 retained organic (pre 0.555 at -0107; final 0.530 at -0110). Batch 2 likewise retained aqueous (0.653 at -0017; 0.657 at -0020). Nonzero final signal assigned to a removed phase was not interpreted as missing inventory or exact carryover because instrument noise and sampling affect closure.

## Scope and unresolved alternatives
All claims concern this simulator, one reagent loading (0.02 mol), explicit aqueous additions, and the tested categorical materials/volumes. Most conditions have n=1; instrument SD is known but process repeatability is not. Phase-volume tests also alter composition, and mixing tests confound time with rpm. Solvent–extractant interaction, equilibrium attainment, separate time/rpm effects, and a general functional law remain unresolved. A future discriminating study would replicate the four 2×2 material cells, vary organic volume while holding solvent/extractant composition constant if legally possible, and independently vary mixing time and speed until a replicated plateau is observed.

payload.report:
Account of partition behavior

Supplied information established that solvent-S0…S3 and extractant-X0…X3 are opaque, independent benchmark labels: matching indices imply no common identity or property, and no property dossier was available. Consequently, I treated materials as categorical and based all mechanistic claims on experiments. The public instrument contract also supplied the relevant uncertainty scales: HPLC standard deviations were 0.015 for each phase-specific product fraction and 0.018 for phase ratio; final-assay uncertainties were 0.010 and 0.012, respectively.

Observations

All baseline comparisons used 0.020 mol reagent, 0.030 L solvent, 0.030 L added aqueous phase, 0.030 L extractant, 120 s mixing at 600 rpm, and 120 s settling. Pre-separation HPLC was used because it observed both phases before either was discarded.

• Solvent screen at X0: batch 1 (S0/X0; event 0007) gave organic/aqueous target fractions 0.195/0.756; batch 2 (S1/X0; event 0017) 0.378/0.653; batch 3 (S2/X0; event 0027) 0.267/0.728; and batch 4 (S3/X0; event 0037) 0.431/0.560. Thus the broad solvent ordering under these conditions was S3 > S1 > S2 > S0 for organic allocation. The S3–S0 contrast, about 0.235, is much larger than the stated HPLC uncertainty.

• Extractant screen at S3: batch 4 (X0) gave organic fraction 0.431, while batches 5–7 gave 0.362 for X1 (event 0047), 0.368 for X2 (0057), and 0.348 for X3 (0067). X0 was distinctly higher in this screen, but the differences among X1, X2, and X3 are too small to rank confidently from single measurements.

• Pairing cross-check: batch 12, S1/X2, gave organic fraction 0.366 and aqueous fraction 0.659 (event 0117). Together with S1/X0 = 0.378, S3/X0 = 0.431, and S3/X2 = 0.368, this forms a 2×2 subset. Its difference-of-differences is approximately −0.051. That is suggestive of a solvent–extractant interaction, but the measurement-only standard deviation of such a four-cell contrast is about 0.030 and no cell was replicated, so interaction is unresolved rather than established.

• Phase-amount tests at S3/X0: batch 8 used 0.015 L each of solvent and extractant with 0.030 L aqueous addition. Its measured phase ratio was 0.228 and its organic/aqueous fractions were 0.332/0.644 (event 0077). Baseline batch 4 had phase ratio 0.327 and fractions 0.431/0.560. Batch 9 used 0.040 L each of solvent and extractant with 0.010 L aqueous addition; its phase ratio was 0.438 and fractions were 0.526/0.456 (event 0087). Organic allocation therefore increased monotonically with measured organic phase share.

• Mixing tests at baseline S3/X0 volumes: weak mixing in batch 10 (1 s, 100 rpm) produced organic/aqueous fractions 0.387/0.624 (event 0097); baseline batch 4 produced 0.431/0.560; and strong mixing in batch 11 (600 s, 1200 rpm) produced 0.555/0.438 (event 0107). The high-minus-baseline organic difference, about 0.124, greatly exceeds measurement noise. No mixing plateau was reached within the tested conditions.

• Phase-retention checks support the interpretation of `separate_phase` as retaining the requested phase. Batch 2 retained aqueous: pre-separation aqueous target was 0.653 and the final assay measured 0.657 (events 0017 and 0020). Batch 10 likewise gave 0.624 before separation and 0.643 after retaining aqueous (0097, 0100). Batch 11 retained organic: 0.555 before separation and 0.530 in the final assay (0107, 0110). These discrepancies are compatible with different instrument noise and sampling. Final phase ratios were correspondingly near zero after aqueous retention and near one after organic retention.

Inference

The strongest account is that target allocation is controlled by three coupled factors: categorical material pairing, available phase amounts, and mixing-dependent transfer. Material effects are large enough that labels cannot be treated as interchangeable. Increasing organic phase share increases the fraction of the fixed target inventory found there. Mixing is not merely an inconsequential handling step: transfer continued to improve beyond 120 s/600 rpm, so baseline measurements should not be described as demonstrated equilibrium values.

A simple concentration-ratio representation is approximately useful but incomplete. From the phase ratios and both phase fractions, the apparent distribution ratio was about 1.74 in batch 8, 1.58 in baseline batch 4, and 1.48 in batch 9. These are of the same order, supporting a partition-like response to phase volume, but their systematic drift argues against claiming one universal constant. Because solvent and extractant volumes changed together in these tests, composition-dependent affinity is an equally plausible explanation.

The paired organic and aqueous signals generally sum near one despite major redistribution—for example, 0.431 + 0.560 in baseline batch 4 and 0.555 + 0.438 in strongly mixed batch 11. This supports redistribution between phases more directly than net creation or destruction of target as the main explanation for the mixing effect, although assay noise prevents exact closure.

Conjecture and uncertain scope

A plausible conjecture is that S3/X0 provides the strongest organic affinity among the tested baseline combinations and that stronger mixing increases approach toward its equilibrium allocation. The data do not show where that equilibrium lies, however. Duration and speed were varied together, so their separate effects, the functional form of mass transfer, and whether still stronger or longer mixing would plateau are unknown.

Other unresolved explanations include genuine solvent–extractant interaction, composition-dependent partition coefficients, phase-volume-dependent nonideality, or condition-dependent process variability. The phase-amount experiments did not hold organic composition constant, and most conditions had only one batch, so process repeatability is not measured. Close material rankings and the 2×2 interaction contrast should therefore remain provisional.

Scope is limited to this synthetic system, 0.020 mol reagent, the tested volumes, one explicit settling time, and the named anonymous materials. Nothing in the supplied information licenses mapping the labels to real substances or extrapolating their ordering outside this domain. Replicated factorial material tests, independent variation of mixing time and rpm, and phase-volume changes at fixed organic composition would be needed to separate the remaining explanations.

payload.rationale: I modeled phase allocation from the measured material-dependent concentration ratio, the extractant share of supplied liquid, and the observed increase with mixing time and speed. Intervals widen for untested solvent–extractant pairs and mixing extrapolations. Q01 is clearly aqueous-dominant. Q05 is provisionally higher than Q06 at the point estimate, but the X3 effect was never measured with S0 and pairing interaction remained unresolved, so D2 is uncertain.

payload.report:
1. Most likely wrong or still untested

No instance-specific prior was supplied. The material packet explicitly provided only opaque categorical labels and no property estimates.

The least tested self-developed law is the prediction model’s assumption that a common mixing response can be transferred across solvent–extractant pairs. The campaign had only three jointly confounded mixing conditions, all for S3/X0: batches 10, 4, and 11 changed both duration and rpm. That evidence showed a mixing effect but did not establish the smooth, transferable response used to extrapolate other materials to 900–1200 s or unfamiliar speeds.

The assumed transfer of the X3 effect from S3 to S0 and S2 is similarly untested. The only X3 screen was batch 7 at S3, while batch 12’s X2 cross-check already suggested possible interaction. A universal or multiplicative material-pair law therefore remains conjectural. The approximately constant distribution-ratio model is also only locally supported; batches 8, 4, and 9 confounded phase amount with organic composition.

2. One additional discriminating experiment

I would run one S0/X3 batch at the Q06 amounts and use staged mixing at one fixed speed. After 120 s at 1200 rpm and settling, I would measure pre-separation HPLC phase ratio and both target fractions. I would then remix the same batch to 900 s cumulative time at 1200 rpm, settle again, and repeat HPLC. The small sampling loss would be recorded and accounted for.

This single-batch trajectory would test two assumptions. Its early absolute allocation would show whether the X3 penalty measured with S3 transfers to S0, while the within-batch change would test whether the strong time response transfers across material pairs without confounding time and rpm.

If the late organic fraction were near the sealed Q06 estimate of about 0.25 and increased substantially with time, I would strengthen the transferable material-factor/mass-transfer explanation. A value near Q05’s estimate, about 0.32, or higher would imply that X3 has little penalty with S0 and would favor pair-specific interaction; a much lower value would imply a stronger adverse S0/X3 interaction. Little change between the two time points would reject the assumed transferable mixing curve and suggest either rapid equilibration or material-specific mixing behavior. A large continued increase would support mass-transfer limitation but still would not prove equilibrium at 900 s.

3. Underused evidence, weak predictions, and consistency audit

The processed phase fractions dominated my analysis. I underused the measured phase-ratio variation across nominally identical baseline volumes, the raw characterization artifacts, and the purity, impurity, and recovery channels. Those channels could help assess whether changes attributed to partition were accompanied by altered target integrity or chromatographic interference. Final assays were used mainly as retention checks; batches 2, 10, and 11 supported phase-selection semantics, but differences between pre-separation HPLC and final assay were not modeled quantitatively. The near-unity sums of the two HPLC phase fractions were informative, but there were no replicate batches to separate process variability from measurement noise.

The least reliable predictions are Q03, Q04, and Q06 because S0/X3 was never observed; Q08, Q11, and Q12 because S2/X3 was also unobserved; and especially Q11 because its 600 s/200 rpm combination lies outside the demonstrated mixing pattern. Q01 and Q03 additionally extrapolate to only 0.008 L extractant, below the campaign’s tested 0.015 L minimum. Q02 and Q05 use the observed S0/X0 pair but still extrapolate strong mixing. Q10 separates long duration from speed in a way the campaign never did. Q09 is comparatively less speculative because its material pair and mixing are closest to batch 1 and the baseline mixing condition, although its phase amounts remain new.

There is a real methodological tension between the sealed report and predictions. The report emphasized that material interaction was unresolved, that no mixing plateau was observed, and that a constant distribution ratio was only approximate. The predictions nevertheless needed point values, so they imposed transferable X3 factors, a smooth mixing extrapolation, and an extractant-share partition relation. Their broad intervals and the ‘uncertain’ Q05-versus-Q06 decision partly acknowledged this, but the point estimates are more structurally committed than the report’s conclusions. The predictions also treated the two noiseless phase fractions as complementary and summing to one; the report only showed approximate experimental closure, not an independently proven exact conservation law. These are prospective modeling assumptions, not conclusions established by the twelve batches.
